source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534

coverage.syllabusAssignment: Presidential removal, independent commissions and modern doctrine
coverage.status: Casebook §7.5.2 covered; assigned 2026 Supreme Court supplements remain pending

topics.title: § 7.5.2a — Removal: Rise of Independent Agencies (pp. 514–520)
topics.description: Decision of 1789, Tenure of Office Act, Myers, Humphrey's Executor, Wiener, structure and reality of independent agencies.

entries.title: President's removal authority and Article II
entries.summary: The federal Constitution generally does not state how to remove officers; the debate is grounded in Article II's vesting and Take Care Clauses, separation of powers, and statutory restrictions.
entries.laymanExplanation: The Constitution lists appointment procedures but barely says how agency officials may be fired.
entries.legalExplanation: Different Supreme Court cases use presidential accountability, statutory text, and agency independence to define removal constraints.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534
entries.examApplication: Identify office, appointing authority, removing authority, statutory for-cause protection, agency structure, and remedy.

entries.title: Decision of 1789
entries.summary: First Congress legislation allowed the President to dismiss the Secretary of State without Senate approval; scholars contest its interpretive significance.
entries.laymanExplanation: The first Congress let the President fire the Secretary without consulting the Senate.
entries.legalExplanation: Whether the episode establishes an original constitutional removal power is historically disputed.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534

entries.title: Tenure of Office Act and Andrew Johnson
entries.summary: The 1867 Act required Senate consent for removal of specified cabinet officers; Johnson's dismissal of his War Secretary triggered impeachment, though the Senate did not convict.
entries.laymanExplanation: A law requiring Senate consent to fire cabinet officials led to a major constitutional crisis.
entries.legalExplanation: The Act was later repealed; later courts questioned such mandatory Senate participation in executive removals.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534

entries.title: Myers v. United States, 272 U.S. 52 (1926)
entries.summary: The Court invalidated a statute requiring Senate consent for removal of a postmaster appointed by the President, emphasizing presidential supervisory authority and faithful execution.
entries.laymanExplanation: The Senate could confirm the postmaster, but couldn't insist on approving the President's firing decision.
entries.legalExplanation: Chief Justice Taft asserted a broad presidential power over executive subordinates; later cases distinguished officials entrusted with independent quasi-legislative or adjudicatory functions.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534
entries.sourceRole: Opinion reasoning excerpted in narrative, not a full standalone opinion
entries.facts: President Wilson discharged an Oregon postmaster despite a statute requiring Senate consent; the postmaster sued for back pay.
entries.issue: May Congress require Senate consent before the President removes an executive officer he appointed?
entries.reasoning: The President's Article II obligation to supervise law execution supports control over executive personnel, including removal.
entries.rule: Congress may not make dismissal of an executive postmaster dependent on Senate consent.
entries.exam: Foundational general principle, not a blanket invalidation of all for-cause protection.
entries.examApplication: Compare the official's executive tasks with independence concerns in Humphrey's Executor and limits refined in Seila Law.
entries.examTrap: Some of Myers's broad historical claims are contested, and its result does not override all later independent-agency cases.

entries.title: Historical criticisms of Myers
entries.summary: The notes report that Congress sometimes imposed removal protections before 1926 and presidents frequently accepted them, complicating Taft's historical account.
entries.laymanExplanation: The textbook warns that the history recounted by Myers was contested, even though the constitutional rule became important.
entries.legalExplanation: This is scholarly context, not an alternate holding.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534

entries.title: Humphrey's Executor v. United States, 295 U.S. 602 (1935)
entries.summary: Congress could protect FTC commissioners from removal except for inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance; Roosevelt's political disagreement with Humphrey was not enough.
entries.laymanExplanation: An FTC commissioner could not be dismissed merely because the President wanted someone who agreed with him.
entries.legalExplanation: The Court distinguished an expert, nonpartisan, multimember commission from Myers's postmaster and upheld statutory independence using the then-prevalent quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial conception.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534
entries.facts: The FTC Act allowed removal for specified cause. Roosevelt requested the resignation of Hoover-appointed FTC Commissioner Humphrey on grounds of political and administrative incompatibility, then removed him; Humphrey's estate sought unpaid salary.
entries.issue: May the President remove a protected FTC commissioner for a political disagreement despite statutory for-cause limits?
entries.holding: No; statutory tenure protection was constitutional and controlled.
entries.reasoning: Congress created the FTC to act impartially as an expert agency and could safeguard independence through removal restrictions; the Court distinguished Myers's purely executive postmaster.
entries.rule: Congress may protect commissioners of the traditional independent-commission type from removal absent specified cause, subject to later Supreme Court treatment of the precedent.
entries.exam: The historically pivotal exception for independent multimember commissions; compare the modern single-director cases.
entries.examApplication: Check actual statutory cause language and the officer/commission structure.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume the 1935 description of agency functions is a complete modern removal test.

entries.title: Independent agencies and for-cause protection
entries.summary: Traditional independent agencies often have protected multimember leadership, staggered terms, and bipartisan membership; executive agencies generally have leadership removable at pleasure.
entries.laymanExplanation: An independent commission usually cannot be completely reshaped overnight through dismissals for political disagreement.
entries.legalExplanation: Tenure protection is a major but not exhaustive indicator of independence; statutory labels alone may be misleading.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534
entries.examApplication: Analyze cause protection, single versus multiple heads, staggered terms, partisan balance, and practical executive influence.

entries.title: Wiener v. United States (1958) — implied adjudicatory tenure
entries.summary: The Court inferred protection against purely political removal for a member of the War Claims Commission even though the statute did not spell out removal standards.
entries.laymanExplanation: An official appointed to resolve war claims according to law was protected against arbitrary replacement by a President.
entries.legalExplanation: The specialized independent adjudicatory function supported implied tenure, but later cases limit indiscriminate extensions.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized in Notes and Questions, not full opinion

entries.title: Practical independence is not absolute
entries.summary: Independent and executive agencies operate under the APA and judicial review, use civil service staffs, and face budgets, appointments, and political pressure; independence is contextual.
entries.laymanExplanation: Even an 'independent' agency remains influenced by politics, budgeting, and presidential chair appointments.
entries.legalExplanation: The text contrasts operational autonomy with modern politicized appointments and discusses Devins/Lewis's empirical critique.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534

entries.title: Independent agencies — normative justifications and critiques
entries.summary: Independence can enhance expertise, continuity, and impartial adjudication, but may reduce presidential democratic accountability or prove ineffective under polarization.
entries.laymanExplanation: Do you want insulated expert decisions or more direct control by an elected President? Both carry costs.
entries.legalExplanation: The notes compare functional and formal approaches and identify the claimed 'independent agency myth' as academic criticism rather than a binding rule.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534

topics.title: § 7.5.2b — Removal: Modern Doctrine (pp. 520–534)
topics.description: Morrison, Seila Law, Collins, Free Enterprise Fund, ALJs, Bowsher, state removal and inferred tenure, assigned PRPA problem.

entries.title: Unitary executive theory
entries.summary: The theory emphasizes presidential ability to supervise executive power as a unified branch through removal and other controls.
entries.laymanExplanation: One elected President should be answerable for executive officers' decisions.
entries.legalExplanation: Modern removal cases frequently adopt accountability rationales associated with this theory.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534

entries.title: Morrison v. Olson (1988) — good-cause independent counsel
entries.summary: The Court upheld removal for good cause by the Attorney General of an independent counsel performing law enforcement, asking whether the restriction unduly impeded constitutional executive duties.
entries.laymanExplanation: The independent prosecutor was allowed some job protection because the Attorney General retained limited oversight.
entries.legalExplanation: The majority moved away from the rigid 'pure executive/quasi' function distinction; Scalia's dissent favored a stronger unitary executive.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534
entries.sourceRole: Summarized with quoted excerpts; full opinion not reproduced here
entries.facts: The Ethics in Government Act permitted a court-appointed independent counsel to investigate federal misconduct and restricted removal by the Attorney General to good cause.
entries.issue: Did for-cause removal protection impermissibly obstruct the President's constitutional law-enforcement obligations?
entries.holding: No, in the circumstances of the case.
entries.reasoning: The Attorney General retained some ability to remove for cause, and Congress sought legitimate independence for the counsel.
entries.rule: Morrison used a functional inquiry into whether removal protection impedes Article II duties; subsequent cases narrowed the approach.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish the holding and Scalia's dissent when discussing evolution of removal doctrine.

entries.title: Seila Law LLC v. CFPB, 591 U.S. 197 (2020)
entries.summary: A powerful federal agency led by one director protected from presidential removal except for cause violated separation of powers; severance of the protection left the CFPB operational.
entries.laymanExplanation: The CFPB could continue regulating, but its single director had to be removable by the President at will.
entries.legalExplanation: Roberts distinguished narrow historical exceptions for multimember independent commissions and some limited-duty inferior officers, emphasizing electoral accountability and concentrated unilateral executive power.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534
entries.facts: The CFPB, created after the financial crisis, was led by a five-year single director protected by statutory cause limits. The Bureau issued a civil investigative demand to Seila Law, which challenged the agency's constitutionality.
entries.issue: Does Congress violate Article II by insulating a single CFPB director wielding significant executive authority, and what remedy is appropriate?
entries.holding: Yes. The single-director for-cause removal restriction was unconstitutional but severable; the agency continued to operate.
entries.reasoning: Executive power must remain accountable through presidential supervision; the insulated director had broad independent rulemaking, adjudicatory, and enforcement authority without multimember checks or annual appropriations dependence.
entries.rule: Seila Law rejects for-cause insulation of the sole director exercising substantial executive power in the CFPB arrangement and leaves traditional precedents for some multimember commissions and inferior officers formally intact.
entries.exam: Compare organizational structure, officer type, statutory cause, and remedy; separate dissenting objections from majority.
entries.examApplication: Draw the chain of control from President to agency head; identify whether an established exception applies.
entries.examTrap: It did not formally overrule Humphrey's Executor or declare all independent agencies unconstitutional.

entries.title: Seila Law — historically recognized exceptions
entries.summary: The majority described traditional for-cause protections for certain multimember expert agencies and for certain inferior officers with limited responsibilities as narrow exceptions to presidential removal authority.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some agency officials may still have tenure protection, but the Court would not extend those examples to the CFPB's sole director.
entries.legalExplanation: These categories reflect the Seila Law opinion and need to be kept separate from later assigned opinions.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534

entries.title: Factors emphasized in Seila Law
entries.summary: Single director, broad regulatory enforcement powers, term longer than the President's, protected removal, and non-annual funding contributed to the Court's structural concern.
entries.laymanExplanation: A powerful and unaccountable sole director differs from a protected group of commissioners.
entries.legalExplanation: The single-head removal protection was central; other structural features strengthened the separation-of-powers analysis.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534

entries.title: Seila Law — Thomas/Gorsuch separate opinion
entries.summary: Thomas and Gorsuch favored reconsidering Humphrey's Executor entirely and challenged the majority's decision to sever the removal restriction.
entries.laymanExplanation: They wanted to go further in strengthening presidential power and disagreed with the fix.
entries.legalExplanation: Their view did not become the holding of the Court.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534

entries.title: Seila Law — Kagan dissent
entries.summary: Kagan argued constitutional text and practice leave substantial flexibility to Congress in creating independent agencies and questioned the single-versus-multimember line.
entries.laymanExplanation: She thought independent agency design was largely for Congress and that one director can be easier to supervise than five.
entries.legalExplanation: She concurred in the severability judgment but dissented on the constitutional merits.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534

entries.title: Collins v. Yellen, 594 U.S. 220 (2021)
entries.summary: The Court extended Seila Law's rule to a smaller single-director agency, the FHFA, and treated an unconstitutional removal restriction differently from an invalid appointment.
entries.laymanExplanation: A smaller agency with one protected director can also violate the President's removal authority.
entries.legalExplanation: The single-director limitation on removal was unconstitutional even though FHFA's functions and budget differed from CFPB's.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534
entries.sourceRole: Detailed notes rather than full case opinion
entries.facts: FHFA was headed by a single director removable only for cause; shareholders challenged the law and agency transactions.
entries.issue: Did the FHFA's more limited authority distinguish Seila Law, and what relief follows the removal defect?
entries.holding: The for-cause restriction was invalid; past agency action was not automatically void.
entries.reasoning: Presidential supervision and public accountability matter for all important executive activity; lawful appointment persists despite later unconstitutional removal insulation.
entries.rule: An invalid single-director removal limit does not automatically invalidate all actions by an otherwise properly appointed official.
entries.examApplication: Separately analyze structural violation, lawfulness of appointment, causal harm, and remedy.

entries.title: Collins remedy — causation and relief
entries.summary: Because the FHFA directors were validly appointed, invalid removal protection did not by itself undo financial transactions; concrete harm related to the inability to remove must be considered.
entries.laymanExplanation: Winning the argument about firing protection does not automatically cancel everything the director already did.
entries.legalExplanation: The Court remanded for harm analysis; plaintiffs failed to prove the required link on remand according to the notes.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534
entries.examTrap: Do not treat unconstitutional removal protection as equivalent to an invalid appointment in every remedial respect.

entries.title: Free Enterprise Fund v. PCAOB, 561 U.S. 477 (2010)
entries.summary: Two successive levels of for-cause protection insulating PCAOB members from presidential supervision violated separation of powers; the subordinate protection was severed.
entries.laymanExplanation: An accounting board cannot be insulated behind both a protected SEC and its own extra firing restrictions in the challenged arrangement.
entries.legalExplanation: The Court assumed protected SEC commissioners, focused on presidential accountability, and declined to rule on every comparable scheme or on ALJs.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534
entries.sourceRole: Substantial excerpts in notes; not a full standalone opinion
entries.facts: Sarbanes-Oxley established PCAOB under SEC oversight; SEC could remove PCAOB members for cause, and SEC members were assumed protected from presidential removal for cause.
entries.issue: Did dual protected removal layers unconstitutionally impede presidential supervision?
entries.reasoning: The President could not hold SEC commissioners responsible for PCAOB actions or compel removal of subordinates except under multiple protected conditions.
entries.rule: The dual for-cause insulation at issue was unconstitutional; severing the lower layer restored supervision.
entries.examApplication: Diagram each officer and removal relationship, distinguish one protective layer from two.
entries.examTrap: The decision reserved the special case of ALJs and did not hold all two-level arrangements automatically invalid.

entries.title: Free Enterprise Fund — Breyer dissent
entries.summary: Breyer emphasized technical expertise and independent adjudication, arguing that one protected SEC layer already constrained the President and removing the second did little in practice.
entries.laymanExplanation: He thought the majority's remedy was formalistic and threatened the independence of administrative judges.
entries.legalExplanation: The dissent cautioned about cascading implications for many government officials.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534

entries.title: ALJ removal protections — issue reserved and circuit disagreement
entries.summary: Free Enterprise Fund expressly did not decide whether its principle governs administrative law judges; Lucia later classified SEC ALJs as officers; the Fifth Circuit's ALJ-removal ruling in Jarkesy was not decided by the Supreme Court.
entries.laymanExplanation: Whether protected administrative judges can have two insulation layers remains a separate issue in this casebook.
entries.legalExplanation: The notes describe circuit disagreement and explain that Jarkesy was affirmed by the Supreme Court on a Seventh Amendment theory.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534
entries.examTrap: SEC v. Jarkesy (2024) did not resolve the ALJ-removal issue despite the circuit holding.

entries.title: Bowsher v. Synar, 478 U.S. 714 (1986)
entries.summary: Congress may not retain the power to remove an officer who executes the law, other than by impeachment; its retained control over the Comptroller General barred assignment of executive deficit-reduction determinations.
entries.laymanExplanation: Congress cannot make someone it can fire the operative executor of its budget-cutting law.
entries.legalExplanation: The Comptroller General's projection and implementation duties amounted to execution; a continuing removal mechanism made him an agent of the legislature.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534
entries.sourceRole: Detailed notes and excerpts, not a full opinion here
entries.facts: The Gramm-Rudman law assigned deficit calculations to the Comptroller General, whom Congress could remove by joint resolution for specified causes.
entries.issue: Could an officer subject to Congress's own removal authority perform executive implementation?
entries.reasoning: Interpreting and applying statutory mandates to implement spending cuts is executive power, which Congress cannot directly control through reserved removal power.
entries.rule: Congress cannot keep formal removal control over officers executing law.
entries.exam: Differentiate congressional removal power from Congress legislatively limiting the President's removal authority.

entries.title: Bowsher — Stevens concurrence
entries.summary: Stevens and Marshall emphasized that the Comptroller General was a congressional agent and could not set binding national policy outside the Article I legislative process.
entries.laymanExplanation: A lawmaking branch cannot use its own employee to impose binding rules instead of passing a law.
entries.legalExplanation: This is an alternative concurrence, not the Burger majority's exact route.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534

entries.title: State removal power varies by constitution
entries.summary: State doctrines are highly jurisdiction-specific; some state courts read gubernatorial powers broadly while others enforce independent-agency tenure more protectively.
entries.laymanExplanation: Different state constitutions can produce different answers about whether a governor can fire agency heads.
entries.legalExplanation: The notes compare Wilcox, Lunding, and statutory cause enforcement decisions.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534
entries.examApplication: Identify jurisdiction and agency's independence before applying federal decisions by analogy.

entries.title: Wilcox versus Lunding — Illinois gubernatorial removal
entries.summary: Older Illinois doctrine allowed broad unreviewable removal; Lunding recognized judicial review for dismissal of an independent elections-board member and distinguished directly responsible executive officers.
entries.laymanExplanation: An independent election commissioner may receive court review even when direct gubernatorial assistants might not.
entries.legalExplanation: The cases illustrate distinctions tied to the kind of state office and its independence.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534

entries.title: Arizona Independent Redistricting Commission v. Brewer
entries.summary: Arizona reinstated a commissioner removed on insufficient stated grounds under a statute allowing dismissal for substantial neglect, gross misconduct, or inability to perform.
entries.laymanExplanation: A governor's objection to a proposed electoral map did not establish the statutory cause required to fire the commission chair.
entries.legalExplanation: The court found asserted meeting and draft-map criticisms did not satisfy legal cause.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534

entries.title: Levy v. Acting Governor — Massachusetts turnpike authority
entries.summary: The Massachusetts court held a policy disagreement about postponing toll increases did not constitute for-cause removal of independently situated authority commissioners.
entries.laymanExplanation: Disagreeing with an independent agency's policy choice isn't always cause to fire its members.
entries.legalExplanation: The majority emphasized autonomy and deliberative decisionmaking; dissenters interpreted fiscal irresponsibility as adequate cause.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534

entries.title: Inferring protection when statutes do not specify cause
entries.summary: The ordinary starting presumption is that removal accompanies appointment, but term length, staggered terms, adjudicative mission, statutory context, and state-specific precedent may affect the result.
entries.laymanExplanation: A five-year appointment doesn't necessarily guarantee the official gets to serve five years.
entries.legalExplanation: Courts often infer at-will removal for indefinite tenure, with more variable outcomes for fixed and staggered terms.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534
entries.examApplication: Analyze express statutory language first, then office duration, agency independence, staggered membership, and judicial precedent.

entries.title: Fixed versus indefinite officer terms
entries.summary: Cases such as Shurtleff and Kalaris illustrate reluctance to infer indefinite life tenure, while FEC-related and staggered-term cases sometimes support inferred protections.
entries.laymanExplanation: An official's term of years can mark the latest end date rather than a shield against earlier dismissal.
entries.legalExplanation: Statutory interpretation depends on agency structure and the relevant jurisdiction; Parsons allows removal of U.S. Attorneys before their fixed term ends.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534

entries.title: 2026 assigned supplements still to be integrated
entries.summary: The syllabus also assigns later opinions on executive removal, including Trump v. Slaughter and Trump v. Cook; those separate materials are not established by this excerpt.
entries.laymanExplanation: The casebook's treatment of older cases does not tell you the outcomes of separately assigned recent opinions.
entries.legalExplanation: Keep this reading's doctrine and later supplemental opinions distinct until the supplements are supplied.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534

problems.title: Publius River Port Authority — Jane's five-year term
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), § 7.5.2, pp. 514–534 (p. 534)
problems.prompt: The Publius River Port Authority (PRPA) operates bridges and port facilities between Madison and Hamilton under a congressionally approved interstate compact, interpreted as federal law. Each state's governor appoints four commissioners. Madison commissioners serve five-year terms subject to state Senate confirmation. Jane was appointed by prior governor Marjorie three years ago. New governor Alex objects to Jane's vote for PRPA chairperson, requests resignation, then threatens removal when she refuses. (a) Jane sues to enjoin her removal; how should the court resolve the dispute? (b) Does the answer change if PRPA is wholly within Madison and established solely under state law? Cf. Pievsky v. Ridge and Alcorn v. Wolfe.
